insider_note: The fraction (2v − 1)/(v² − v) integrates directly to log(v² − v) because the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator — spotting that match saves working out a full partial-fraction split.

steps.label: Recognise homogeneous form and substitute
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Every term is degree 2 in x and y, so the equation is homogeneous.
steps.memory_tip: y², xy and x² are all degree 2 — homogeneous of degree 2.
lines: Take the dy term across and divide by dx:
Every term top and bottom has degree 2, so

lines.text: this is a homogeneous D.E. Put y = vx

steps.why: Moving (2xy − x²)dy across the equals sign and dividing every term by x² after substituting y = vx reduces the whole right side to a function of v alone, confirming the homogeneous form.
common_mistakes: Losing the minus sign when moving (2xy − x²)dy to the other side.
Miscanceling x² in the numerator against x² in the denominator.

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Subtract v as a fraction with denominator (1 − 2v).
steps.memory_tip: v(1 − 2v) = v − 2v² is the term that combines with v² − 2v to give 3v² − 3v.

lines.text: Take v to the right side:

steps.why: Writing v as v(1 − 2v)/(1 − 2v) puts both terms over the same denominator, and expanding v² − 2v − v + 2v² leaves 3v² − 3v; flipping the sign on both sides keeps the numerator (2v − 1) matched with the denominator's derivative in the next step.
common_mistakes: Losing the −v term when expanding v(1 − 2v) = v − 2v².
Forgetting to flip the overall sign when rewriting (1 − 2v) as −(2v − 1).

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The numerator (2v − 1) is exactly the derivative of the denominator (v² − v) once the constant 3 is pulled out.
steps.memory_tip: d/dv(v² − v) = 2v − 1 — a direct log-integral shape.

lines.text: 2v − 1 is the derivative of v² − v:
Multiply by 3; 3 log c = log c³, and c₁ = c³:

steps.why: Since 2v − 1 is the exact derivative of v² − v, the left integral is a direct log; multiplying the whole equation by 3 afterwards clears the fraction in front of the log, matching the form needed to compare with the right side.
common_mistakes: Missing the factor of 3 in the denominator and integrating (2v−1)/(v²−v) directly without the 1/3.
Forgetting to multiply the constant of integration by 3 along with the rest of the equation.

steps.label: Return to x and y
steps.margin_note: One mark. Remove the log by exponentiating, then substitute v = y/x.
steps.memory_tip: v² − v = c/x³ is the general family in v — substitute v = y/x and multiply through by x³ next.
steps.why: Exponentiating removes the log, giving the family of solutions in v directly; substituting v = y/x then carries that family back into the original variables x and y.
common_mistakes: Substituting v = y/x before exponentiating, leaving a log with a fraction inside it.
Writing v² − v as (v − 1)² by mistake.

steps.label: Final equation
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Multiply through by x³ to clear every denominator at once.
steps.memory_tip: x³·(y²/x² − y/x) = x³·c/x³ = c — multiplying by x³ clears both fractions on the left in one move.

lines.text: and taking out y gives xy(y − x):

steps.why: Multiplying through by x³ clears the fractions on both sides at once, and factoring out xy from y² − xy gives the compact final relation the examiner expects.
common_mistakes: Multiplying by the wrong power of x and leaving one fraction uncleared.
Leaving the answer as x(y² − xy) = c instead of factoring to xy(y − x) = c.
